summary: Clarifies how addresses and identifiers should be used in GMPLS networks to help different vendors' routers interwork. Based on implementation and deployment experience, it explains how to interpret address fields and which addresses to place in them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An instruction sheet on which address goes in which box, so machines from different makers agree.

questions: how to interpret address fields in gmpls
subtitle: Address usage rules for GMPLS network routers

tldr.problem: GMPLS networks use many types of addresses and identifiers, causing confusion when routers from different vendors try to interwork and agree on which addresses to use in which fields.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies how to interpret and use address fields in GMPLS protocols (RSVP-TE, OSPF, IS-IS), distinguishing between numbered and unnumbered links, and showing how to handle IPv6 addresses in management systems.
tldr.outcome: Provides practical guidance based on implementation and deployment experience to help vendors implement interoperable GMPLS routers.

today: RFC 4990 remains an informational reference for GMPLS implementations. While GMPLS adoption has been more limited than initially expected, implementations that do use GMPLS generally follow the guidance in this RFC for address handling to ensure interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a system for setting up and controlling connections in networks that handle multiple types of traffic: packet data, time division multiplexing, wavelengths, and other switching types. Unlike plain MPLS which works with packet-switched networks, GMPLS works across diverse technologies.

GMPLS uses several protocols (RSVP-TE for signaling, OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE for routing) that refer to many different types of addresses. This document clarifies how to use these addresses in practice, based on real implementation and interoperability testing experience. It does not define new procedures but clarifies how to apply existing specifications correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS is like a language different routers use to reserve paths through networks. Different vendors were saying the same thing in different ways, so this document explains the common way to do it.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Address Types
sections.content:
GMPLS networks separate data plane resources (the physical equipment and links that carry traffic) from control plane resources (the software that manages which paths packets take). The control plane includes both signaling (RSVP-TE) and routing (OSPF-TE, IS-IS-TE) components.

TE Router ID: A stable IP address at each GMPLS router that is always reachable as long as the router has any IP connectivity. This is typically a loopback address. It identifies the router in the control plane and serves as a stable reference point regardless of which interface might be down.

Numbered Links: Links where each end has an IP address. The local interface gets one address, the remote interface gets another. These addresses must be unique within the network but do not need to be globally routable.

Unnumbered Links: Links identified by a combination of the TE Router ID of the local router and a link-local interface ID (a number unique only within that router). This saves IP address space for links that are only used internally.

GMPLS supports both numbered and unnumbered addressing simultaneously. A router must be able to send and process messages with either type, even if it only uses one type internally.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router has a stable phone number (TE Router ID). Links can either have their own addresses (numbered) or just router numbers plus a port number (unnumbered). All routers must understand both.

sections.title: Address Fields in Protocol Messages
sections.content:
RSVP-TE messages carry several address fields that serve different purposes. The Session Object contains the tunnel endpoint address (where the connection ends) and must be set to the TE Router ID of the destination router or, if known, the destination data plane interface address.

The Sender Template Object contains the tunnel sender address, typically the TE Router ID of the ingress router. For tunnels creating Forwarding Adjacencies, it should be set to the head-end address so the tail-end address can be inferred.

The RSVP_HOP Object contains the IP address of the sender of the message (a reachable control plane address, ideally the TE Router ID for stability) and optionally an Interface ID identifying the associated data channel.

Explicit Route Objects (ERO): These specify the path the connection should take. Subobjects in the ERO can identify abstract nodes, specific routers by TE Router ID, or specific links. Strict hops mean the connection must go directly to the specified next hop; loose hops allow intervening routers.

Record Route Objects (RRO): These record the path actually taken by the connection as it is established. Each router adds information about itself and the link it used. The RRO allows operators to verify the path and can be used as an ERO to recreate a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages have fields for 'where we're going', 'who we are', 'the path to follow', and 'the path we took'. Using the right address in each field is crucial for routers to work together.

sections.title: Control Plane and Data Plane Separation
sections.content:
GMPLS supports separating the control plane (where routers negotiate paths) from the data plane (where traffic flows). The two planes can use different physical paths and addresses.

A native control plane uses standard IP forwarding to deliver RSVP-TE messages between routers. Messages traverse the normal IP network and are not tunneled.

A tunneled control plane encapsulates RSVP-TE messages inside another tunnel (IP-in-IP, GRE, or MPLS) so that two adjacent routers in the data plane can be multiple IP hops apart in the control plane. This allows the control plane to be physically separate from the data plane.

One critical security issue found in interoperability testing: control channels must not be used for forwarding user data. Some implementations mistakenly set both control and data plane addresses to the same value, accidentally creating parallel interfaces with identical addresses. Operators must keep control and data plane addresses strictly separate.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages and data can travel different paths and use different addresses. But if someone accidentally mixes them, traffic might take the wrong route. These should always be kept apart.

sections.title: IPv6 in Management Systems
sections.content:
GMPLS management uses MIB (Management Information Base) modules where operators configure and monitor tunnels. Many MIB objects are limited to 32-bit values, but IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

When configuring a tunnel with IPv6 source and destination addresses, operators should configure an explicit route in the MIB tunnel hop table with the IPv6 addresses as the first and last hops, even though a 32-bit LSR ID is used for identification in the main tunnel table. The ingress router then extracts the IPv6 addresses from the configured hop entries and uses them in the signaling messages.

This approach allows operators to manage GMPLS tunnels with IPv6 endpoints while the MIB itself continues to use 32-bit router identifiers. It requires that the router support explicit route configuration in the hop table.
sections.plainLanguage: Old management systems only hold 32-bit numbers for addresses, but IPv6 is bigger. The trick is to store the big IPv6 address in a different place (the hop list) and copy it into the actual messages when needed.
